items.title: Read the throughput quotas of your account
items.kills: "A DynamoDB table has no throughput limit."
items.read_only_alternative: This task is read-only. It needs no alternative.

steps.text: Open AWS CloudShell. Read the provisioned throughput quotas of your account in this Region: one pair for the whole account, and one pair for each new table.
steps.expect: Four numbers: AccountMaxReadCapacityUnits, AccountMaxWriteCapacityUnits, TableMaxReadCapacityUnits and TableMaxWriteCapacityUnits. With the default quotas, the two account values are 80,000 and the two table values are 40,000. You can ask AWS to raise each of them.

steps.text: Run the same command for a second Region, <OTHER_REGION>. Choose a Region that you do not work in, for example eu-west-1.
steps.expect: The four numbers of that Region. Each Region shows its own set, because DynamoDB quotas apply per Region.

steps.text: List the default DynamoDB quotas of this Region. Find the rows whose names hold the words throughput limit.
steps.expect: A table of quota names, default values, and True or False. True marks a quota that you can ask AWS to increase. In on-demand mode, the account has no account-level throughput quota, but each table has one: the default is 40,000 read request units and 40,000 write request units.

items.title: Compare a Query and a Scan with consumed capacity shown
items.kills: "A filter expression makes a Scan read less and cost less."
items.cost: $0 in practice. On-demand mode is billed per read or write request, and this task makes a few small requests on three tiny items.
items.cost_if_forgotten: $0 a day for throughput: an on-demand table with no traffic is not charged for throughput. The few bytes of the three items round to $0 for storage.
items.read_only_alternative: These steps need no AWS resources. Answer the predict question of step 5 on paper. Then find the example To scan a table on the AWS CLI Command Reference page for aws dynamodb scan. That scan filters by Artist, and its output shows Count 2 and ScannedCount 3. Compare the two numbers, as in step 5.

steps.text: Open AWS CloudShell. Create an on-demand table with a partition key pk and a sort key sk, tagged for this book and this task. In the command, HASH marks the partition key and RANGE marks the sort key.
steps.command: aws dynamodb create-table --table-name saa-dynamodb-t02 --attribute-definitions AttributeName=pk,AttributeType=S AttributeName=sk,AttributeType=S --key-schema AttributeName=pk,KeyType=HASH AttributeName=sk,KeyType=RANGE --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST --tags Key=book,Value=saa Key=task,Value=dynamodb-t02 --query "TableDescription.TableStatus"
steps.expect: CREATING: the status of the new table.

steps.text: Wait until the table is ready.
steps.expect: No output when the table status is ACTIVE.

steps.text: Write three small items in one request: two items with pk a, and one item with pk b.
steps.expect: UnprocessedItems with an empty value: DynamoDB wrote all three items. If the value is not empty, run the command again.

steps.text: Scan the whole table and show the consumed capacity. Count is the number of items returned. ScannedCount is the number of items that the Scan evaluated before any filter.
steps.expect: Count 3, ScannedCount 3, and a Units value. Note the Units value for the next step.

steps.text: Scan again, now with a filter expression that keeps the items with pk a.
steps.expect: Count 2, ScannedCount 3, and the same Units value as in step 4. The filter changed the answer, not the read.
steps.predict: The filter keeps two of the three items. Does this Scan read fewer items and use less read capacity than the Scan of step 4?
steps.explain: A Scan [reads every item in a table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-reads-every-item). The filter runs after the Scan reads the items, so the Scan [consumes the same amount of read capacity](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-filter-same-read-capacity) with or without the filter. Read capacity depends on [the number of items and the size](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-read-capacity-by-items-read-not-returned) of the items read, [not on the amount of data](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-read-capacity-by-items-read-not-returned) returned.

steps.text: Fix it: ask for the items of pk a with a Query. The key condition names one partition key value, so DynamoDB reads the items of that one partition key.
steps.expect: Count 2 and ScannedCount 2: the Query evaluated the two items of pk a and no other item. With three tiny items, Units can equal the value of the Scan. On a large table, the Scan reads every item, and the gap grows.

cleanup.text: Delete the table and its items.
Wait until the table no longer exists.

verify.expect: An error that names ResourceNotFoundException. The table is gone.

still_costs: Nothing that grows in a day: an on-demand table with no traffic is not charged for throughput, and the few bytes of three tiny items round to $0. Delete the table anyway, so that the next run of this task can use the same name.
If the CloudShell session ended before the cleanup, the cleanup commands still work: they name the table and use no variable.

items.title: Make a conditional write refuse an overwrite
items.kills: "A second PutItem with the same key fails on its own."
items.cost: $0 in practice. On-demand mode is billed per read or write request, and this task makes a few small requests on one tiny item.
items.cost_if_forgotten: $0 a day for throughput: an on-demand table with no traffic is not charged for throughput. The few bytes of the item round to $0 for storage.
items.read_only_alternative: These steps need no AWS resources. Answer the predict question of step 4 on paper. Then find the section Conditional put on the page DynamoDB condition expression CLI example in the Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide. Its put-item example uses attribute_not_exists(Id) to refuse an overwrite. Compare it with step 5.

steps.text: Open AWS CloudShell. Create an on-demand table with one key attribute, the partition key pk, tagged for this book and this task. Each item is one job record.
steps.command: aws dynamodb create-table --table-name saa-dynamodb-t03 --attribute-definitions AttributeName=pk,AttributeType=S --key-schema AttributeName=pk,KeyType=HASH --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST --tags Key=book,Value=saa Key=task,Value=dynamodb-t03 --query "TableDescription.TableStatus"
steps.expect: CREATING: the status of the new table.

steps.text: Wait until the table is ready.
steps.expect: No output when the table status is ACTIVE.

steps.text: Write the first job record: pk job1 with status new.
A second worker writes the same job with status done. Ask DynamoDB to return the old item if this write replaces one.
steps.expect: No error. The output shows Attributes with status new: the old item, which this write replaced.
steps.predict: An item with pk job1 already exists. Will this second write with the same key fail?
steps.explain: By default, PutItem is [unconditional](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-writes-unconditional-by-default): it [overwrites an existing item](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-writes-unconditional-by-default) that has the same primary key. The second write returned no error, and the first record of job1 is gone. A conditional write can stop this: a PutItem that succeeds [if there is not already an item](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-conditional-write-use-cases) with the same primary key.

steps.text: Fix it: write job1 again, with the condition attribute_not_exists(pk). The condition lets the write run when no item with this key exists yet.
steps.expect: An error that names ConditionalCheckFailedException, with the message The conditional request failed. DynamoDB refused the write. With this condition, the write of step 4 would have failed in the same way.

steps.text: Read the item with a strongly consistent read, so that the answer reflects every earlier successful write.
steps.expect: The item job1 with status done. The refused write of step 5 changed nothing.

cleanup.text: Wait until the table no longer exists.

verify.expect: An error that names ResourceNotFoundException. The table is gone.

still_costs: Nothing that grows in a day: an on-demand table with no traffic is not charged for throughput, and the few bytes of one tiny item round to $0. Delete the table anyway, so that the next run of this task can use the same name.
If the CloudShell session ended before the cleanup, the cleanup commands still work: they name the table and use no variable.
